title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) for Intent-to-Configuration NetOps: Null Results on a Synthetic Verifier-Checked Task Bank
abstract: We conducted a preregistered, fully autonomous paired experiment to evaluate whether interposing a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) reduces verifier-detected semantic invariant violations when translating operator intents into device configurations. Using a public synthetic NetOps task bank (N = 240 paired tasks), a pybatfish-style deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and gpt-5-mini as the generator, we compared (A) unconstrained generation, (B) schema-constrained decoding, and (C) the GVR intervention (one repair attempt permitted). The preregistered primary estimand was the paired difference in verifier-detected violation rate (C minus baseline). All 240 paired tasks completed without infrastructure failures. Every generated candidate in both baseline and guarded (GVR) arms satisfied the deterministic verifier (n11 = 240, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). The paired estimate is 0.0 (exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; 95% paired-bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.0]). In these verifier-checked synthetic tasks, GVR did not improve the already-perfect verifier acceptance rate; repair was not applied because initial candidates already satisfied verifier predicates. We analyze causes (task/verifier strength, limited repair budget, single-model scope), discuss operational implications, and outline reproducible directions (adversarial task injection, multiple models/validators, semantic oracle strengthening) needed before claiming operational reliability of agentic NetOps pipelines.

sections.introduction: Automating intent-to-configuration translation is an increasingly important NetOps use case for large language models (LLMs) and agentic pipelines. Prior work documents pervasive LLM hallucination in code and tool-calling contexts and recommends interposing deterministic validators and repair cycles (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) to reduce mechanically checkable defects [Cadenas 2026; Zhang et al. 2025; Huang et al. 2026]. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment that asks: Does deterministic verification plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop reduce verifier-detected semantic invariant violations relative to (A) unconstrained LLM generation and (B) schema-constrained decoding? Our contributions are: (1) a machine-readable preregistration and executed paired experiment (N=240 tasks) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic NetOps validator; (2) a statistically exact confirmatory analysis of the primary estimand; and (3) a diagnostic failure-mode analysis and reproducible implications for future NetOps evaluations.
sections.related_work: LLM failures in operational settings (hallucination, incorrect tool calls, fabricated identifiers) are well documented across code-generation and agentic pipelines [Peng et al. 2026; Akindurodoye 2026; Huang et al. 2026]. Architectures that insert deterministic verification oracles between stochastic generation and acceptance (Generate–Verify–Repair) have been proposed and studied in regulated-code and software-generation use cases, showing improvements for mechanically checkable properties such as compilation and test passing [Cadenas 2026; Yang et al. 2026]. Constraining generation with schemas, grammar-constrained decoding, or constraint‑based adaptation increases syntactic/executable output rates but does not by itself guarantee domain-level semantic correctness across arbitrary topologies [ChemRxiv 2026; Schmidt & Cimiano 2024]. Prior NetOps systems (e.g., Confucius, MeshAgent) emphasize integrating validators and human oversight to avoid regressions, but controlled preregistered paired evaluations of GVR versus strong baselines have been scarce [Wang et al. 2024; Zhou et al. 2025]. Our study situates itself at this gap: a preregistered, paired, verifier-grounded confirmatory test of GVR for intent-to-configuration NetOps.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: We froze a preregistration (study_id c1_gvr_semantic_eval_prereg_v1) before execution. The public synthetic NetOps task bank comprised 12 topology/policy clusters × 20 tasks = 240 tasks. Each task provided: an initial device state, a natural-language intent, required safety/workflow constraints, and an expected final state. The primary estimand was the paired difference in verifier-detected semantic-violation rate (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). Two prespecified primary comparisons were registered: (C vs A) guarded (GVR) vs unconstrained baseline, and (C vs B) guarded vs schema-constrained baseline; Bonferroni correction across the two comparisons was applied (family alpha = 0.05 → per-comparison alpha = 0.025). Execution contract: adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; model: gpt-5-mini (requested); generation budget: at most one initial generation and at most one repair call per task; maximum_model_calls = 480; deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (pybatfish-style diagnostics: reachability matrix, ACL-violation lists, counterexample flows). Repair policy: single bounded repair iteration with edit-budget constraints (documented in the preregistration). Analysis plan: paired McNemar-style exact test via the registered executor paired_binary_analysis_v1, compute absolute risk reduction and 95% Wilson/bootstrap CIs; conservative sensitivity analyses for infrastructure failures were preregistered.
sections.results: Execution completed as preregistered (execution manifest timestamps and artifacts archived). All 240 paired tasks ran to completion with no infrastructure/model-call failures and no flagged contamination items. Verifier outcome (binary: verifier-detected semantic violation) was negative for every generated candidate in both baseline and guarded conditions: n11 = 240 (both accepted), n10 = n01 = n00 = 0. The paired estimate (rate_guarded − rate_baseline) = 0.0. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap resamples = 10,000). Repair application: repair_applied = false for all episodes because the shared initial candidate already satisfied validator predicates; therefore no repair iteration produced changed artifacts. Secondary and sensitivity analyses (cluster stratification, flagged-item sensitivities) are reported in the archived analysis artifacts; none altered the primary null outcome.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: In this preregistered synthetic evaluation, GVR provided no reduction in verifier-detected semantic violations because the generator produced verifier-compliant configurations at the initial generation step in every case. This null result has two non-exclusive explanations: (1) the synthetic task bank and the deterministic validator together defined predicates that gpt-5-mini (with the supplied prompts) could satisfy reliably, making repair unnecessary; (2) the tasks may underrepresent adversarial or out-of-distribution challenges where GVR could add value. Operational implications: a GVR pipeline can be redundant when generator+prompting already meets verifier predicates for routine tasks, but relying on that observation without adversarial validation risks overconfidence. The absence of repairs here does not imply universal safety: verifier incompleteness (unobserved semantic properties), single-model dependence, and synthetic-data external‑validity limits remain important. Recommended next steps: (i) inject adversarially crafted and vendor-diverse tasks that exercise semantic invariants beyond the current verifier predicates; (ii) evaluate multiple generator families and stronger semantic or formal verifiers (SMT/constraint hybrids) to measure cross-model robustness; (iii) measure human-in-the-loop utility and operational throughput trade-offs when GVR triggers human review.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, autonomous paired experiment comparing GVR to strong baselines on a public synthetic NetOps task bank. All generated candidates passed a deterministic verifier in both baseline and guarded arms (n = 240 pairs), producing a null confirmatory result: GVR did not improve verifier-detected semantic-violation rates under these conditions. The artifacts, analysis, and logs are archived. This outcome highlights that (a) strong baselines plus precise verifier predicates can make repair loops unnecessary on some task distributions, and (b) rigorous adversarial and cross-model evaluations remain essential before claiming operational reliability for agentic NetOps pipelines.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and verifier scope: the N = 240 tasks were synthetic and verified against a pybatfish-style deterministic validator; results may not generalize to production topologies, vendor-specific syntax, or richer semantic invariants not encoded in the verifier.
Single-model evaluation: the experiment used one generator (gpt-5-mini). Results do not establish cross-model generality.
Repair budget and policy: only a single bounded repair iteration was permitted by design; different repair budgets or iterative strategies could produce different outcomes.

Verifier completeness risk: passing the deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks (unobserved invariants, emergent behaviors, or properties outside the verifier model).
Adversarial robustness: the task bank did not include adversarially crafted counterexamples intended specifically to induce hallucination or oracle-overfitting; adversarial evaluations are needed.
